entries.0392dc89ec3167ba6421ea08a22e856dad4846d5: <div sID="gen1546" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Exod.6" sID="Exod.6"/> <div eID="gen1546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1547" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1548" type="x-p"/> Much ado there was to bring Moses to his work, and when the ice was broken, some difficulty having occurred in carrying it on, there was no less ado to put him forward in it. Witness this chapter, in which, I. God satisfies Moses himself in an answer to his complaints in the close of the foregoing chapter, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. He gives him fuller instructions than had yet been given him what to say to the children of Israel, for their satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.2-Exod.6.8">ver. 2-8</reference>), but to little purpose, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">ver. 9</reference>. III. He sends him again to Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.10-Exod.6.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. But Moses objects against (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">ver. 12</reference>), upon which a very strict charge is given to him and his brother to execute their commission with vigour, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">ver. 13</reference>. IV. Here is an abstract of the genealogy of the tribes of Reuben and Simeon, to introduce that of Levi, that the pedigree of Moses and Aaron might be cleared (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.14-Exod.6.25">ver. 14-25</reference>), and then the chapter concludes with a repetition of so much of the preceding story as was necessary to make way for the following chapter.
entries.71bfb9639c8f75c134007eba8160775ca0052530: <div eID="gen1548" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1547" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Promise of Deliverance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh: for with a strong hand shall he let them go, and with a strong hand shall he drive them out of his land. <hi type="super">2</hi> And God spake unto Moses, and said unto him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">3</hi> And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, by <hi type="italic">the name of</hi> God Almighty, but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them. <hi type="super">4</hi> And I have also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimage, wherein they were strangers. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians keep in bondage; and I have remembered my covenant. 6 Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments: <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God: and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which bringeth you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will bring you in unto the land, concerning the which I did swear to give it to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; and I will give it you for an heritage: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And Moses spake so unto the children of Israel: but they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit, and for cruel bondage. <div eID="gen1549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1550" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God silences Moses's complaints with the assurance of success in this negotiation, repeating the promise made him in <reference osisRef="Exod.3.20">ch. iii. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">After that, he will let you go.</hi> When Moses was at his wit's end, wishing he had staid in Midian, rather than have come to Egypt to make bad worse—when he was quite at a loss what to do—<hi type="italic">Then the Lord said unto Moses,</hi> for the quieting of his mind, "<hi type="italic">Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.1">v. 1</reference>); now that the affair has come to a crisis, things are as bad as they can be, Pharaoh is in the height of pride and Israel in the depth of misery, now is my time to appear." See <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Ps. xii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Now will I arise.</hi> Note, Man's extremity is God's opportunity of helping and saving. Moses had been expecting what God would do; but now he shall see what he will do, shall see his day at length, <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job xxiv. 1</reference>. Moses had been trying what he could do, and could effect nothing. "Well," says God, "now thou shalt see what <hi type="italic">I</hi> will do; let me alone to deal with this proud man," <reference osisRef="Job.40.12-Job.40.13">Job xl. 12, 13</reference>. Note, Then the deliverance of God's church will be accomplished, when God takes the work into his own hands. <hi type="italic">With a strong hand,</hi> that is, being forced to it by a strong hand, <hi type="italic">he shall let them go.</hi> Note, As some are brought to their duty by the strong hand of God's grace, who are made willing in the day of his power, so others by the strong hand of his justice, breaking those that would not bend. <div eID="gen1550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1551" type="x-p"/> II. He gives him further instructions, that both he and the people of Israel might be encouraged to hope for a glorious issue of this affair. Take comfort, <div eID="gen1551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1552" type="x-p"/> 1. From God's name, Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.2-Exod.6.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He begins with this, <hi type="italic">I am Jehovah,</hi> the same with, <hi type="italic">I am that I am,</hi> the fountain of being, and blessedness, and infinite perfection. The patriarchs knew this name, but they did not know him in this matter by that which this name signifies. God would now be known by his name <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> that is, (1.) A God performing what he had promised, and so inspiring confidence in his promises. (2.) A God perfecting what he had begun, and finishing his own work. In the history of the creation, God is never called Jehovah till the heavens and the earth were finished, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen. ii. 4</reference>. When the salvation of the saints is completed in eternal life, then he will be known by his name Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.13">Rev. xxii. 13</reference>); in the meantime they shall find him, for their strength and support, <hi type="italic">El-shaddai, a God all-sufficient,</hi> a God that is enough and will be so, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.20">Mic. vii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen1552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1553" type="x-p"/> 2. From his covenant: <hi type="italic">I have established my covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.6.4">v. 4</reference>. Note, The covenants God makes he establishes; they are made as firm as the power and truth of God can make them. We may venture our all upon this bottom. <div eID="gen1553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1554" type="x-p"/> 3. From his compassions (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel;</hi> he means their groaning on occasion of the late hardships put upon them. Note, God take notice of the increase of his people's calamities, and observes how their enemies grow upon them. <div eID="gen1554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1555" type="x-p"/> 4. From his present resolutions, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.6-Exod.6.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Here is line upon line, to assure them that they should be brought triumphantly out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">v. 6</reference>), and should be put in possession of the land of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bring you out. I will rid you. I will redeem you. I will bring you into the land of Canaan,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I will give it to you.</hi> Let man take the shame of his unbelief, which needs such repetitions; and let God have the glory of his condescending grace, which gives us such repeated assurances for our satisfaction. <div eID="gen1555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1556" type="x-p"/> 5. From his gracious intentions in all these, which were great, and worthy of him, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.7">v. 7</reference>. (1.) He intended their happiness: <hi type="italic">I will take you to me for a people,</hi> a peculiar people, and <hi type="italic">I will be to you a God;</hi> more than this we need not ask, we cannot have, to make us happy. (2.) He intended his own glory: <hi type="italic">You shall know that I am the Lord.</hi> God will attain his own ends, nor shall we come short of them if we make them our chief end too. Now, one would think, these good words, and comfortable words, should have revived the drooping Israelites, and cause them to forget their misery; but, on the contrary, their miseries made them regardless of God's promises (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They harkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit.</hi> That is, [1.] They were so taken up with their troubles that they did not heed him. [2.] They were so cast down with their late disappointment that they did not believe him. [3.] They had such a dread of Pharaoh's power and wrath that they durst not themselves move in the least towards their deliverance. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Disconsolate spirits often put from them the comforts they are entitled to, and stand in their own light. See <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Isa. xxviii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Strong passions oppose strong consolations. By indulging ourselves in discontent and fretfulness, we deprive ourselves of the comfort we might have both from God's word and from his providence, and must thank ourselves if we go comfortless.
entries.bd7b6e470bb5576ed41e213421481166aafd5057: <div eID="gen1556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">11</hi> Go in, speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land. 12 And Moses spake before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Behold, the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me; how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who <hi type="italic">am</hi> of uncircumcised lips? <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, and gave them a charge unto the children of Israel, and unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt. <div eID="gen1557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1558" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God sends Moses the second time to Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.11">v. 11</reference>) upon the same errand as before, to command him, at his peril, that he <hi type="italic">let the children of Israel go.</hi> Note, God repeats his precepts before he begins his punishments. Those that have often been called in vain to leave their sins must yet be called again and again, whether they will hear or whether they will forbear, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.1">Ezek. iii. 11</reference>. God is said to <hi type="italic">hew</hi> sinners by his prophets (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.5">Hos. vi. 5</reference>), which denotes the repetition of the strokes. <hi type="italic">How often would I have gathered you?</hi> <div eID="gen1558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1559" type="x-p"/> II. Moses makes objections, as one discouraged, and willing to give up the cause, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">v. 12</reference>. He pleads, 1. The unlikelihood of Pharaoh's hearing: "<hi type="italic">Behold the children of Israel have not hearkened unto me;</hi> they give no heed, no credit, to what I have said; how then can I expect that Pharaoh should hear me? If the anguish of their spirit makes them deaf to that which would compose and comfort them, much more will the anger of his spirit, his pride and insolence, make him deaf to that which will but exasperate and provoke him." If God's professing people hear not his messengers, how can it be thought that his professed enemy should? Note, The frowardness and untractableness of those that are called Christians greatly discourage ministers, and make them ready to despair of success in dealing with those that are atheistical and profane. We would be instrumental to unite Israelites, to refine and purify them, to comfort and pacify them; but, if they hearken not to us, how shall we prevail with those in whom we cannot pretend to such an interest? But with God all things are possible. 2. He pleads the unreadiness and infirmity of his own speaking: <hi type="italic">I am of uncircumcised lips;</hi> it is repeated, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.30">v. 30</reference>. He was conscious to himself that he had not the gift of utterance, had no command of language; his talent did not lie that way. To this objection God had given a sufficient answer before, and therefore he ought not to have insisted upon it, for the sufficiency of grace can supply the defects of nature at any time. Note, Though our infirmities ought to humble us, yet they ought not to discourage us from doing our best in any service we have to do for God. His strength is made perfect in our weakness. <div eID="gen1559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1560" type="x-p"/> III. God again joins Aaron in commission with Moses, and puts an end to the dispute by interposing his own authority, and giving them both a solemn charge, upon their allegiance to their great Lord, to execute it with all possible expedition and fidelity. When Moses repeats his baffled arguments, he shall be argued with no longer, but God gives him a charge, and Aaron with him, both to the children of Israel and to Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, God's authority is sufficient to answer all objections, and binds us to obedience, without murmuring or disputing, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.14">Phil. ii. 14</reference>. Moses himself has need to be charged, and so has Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1 Tim. vi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1">2 Tim. iv. 1</reference>.
entries.cb6e872fc3bb4f9c658b08791baaf6960ff59e71: <div eID="gen1560" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1561" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> These <hi type="italic">be</hi> the heads of their fathers' houses: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel; Hanoch, and Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi: these <hi type="italic">be</hi> the families of Reuben. 15 And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the families of Simeon. <hi type="super">16</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations; Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari: and the years of the life of Levi <hi type="italic">were</hi> an hundred thirty and seven years. <hi type="super">17</hi> The sons of Gershon; Libni, and Shimi, according to their families. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath <hi type="italic">were</hi> an hundred thirty and three years. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the sons of Merari; Mahali and Mushi: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the families of Levi according to their generations. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram <hi type="italic">were</hi> an hundred and thirty and seven years. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the sons of Uzziel; Mishael, and Elzaphan, and Zithri. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the sons of Korah; Assir, and Elkanah, and Abiasaph: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the families of the Korhites. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Eleazar Aaron's son took him <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the daughters of Putiel to wife; and she bare him Phinehas: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the heads of the fathers of the Levites according to their families. <hi type="super">26</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> that Aaron and Moses, to whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Bring out the children of Israel from the land of Egypt according to their armies. <hi type="super">27</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> they which spake to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring out the children of Israel from Egypt: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> that Moses and Aaron. <hi type="super">28</hi> And it came to pass on the day <hi type="italic">when</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses in the land of Egypt, <hi type="super">29</hi> That the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : speak thou unto Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say unto thee. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses said before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> of uncircumcised lips, and how shall Pharaoh hearken unto me? <div eID="gen1561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1562" type="x-p"/> I. We have here a genealogy, not an endless one, such as the apostle condemns (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1 Tim. i. 4</reference>), for it ends in those two great patriots Moses and Aaron, and comes in here to show that they were Israelites, bone of their bone and flesh of their flesh whom they were sent to deliver, raised up unto them of their brethren, as Christ also should be, who was to be the prophet and priest, the Redeemer and lawgiver, of the people of Israel, and whose genealogy also, like this, was to be carefully preserved. The heads of the houses of three of the tribes are here named, agreeing with the accounts we had, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1-Gen.46.34">Gen. 46</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot thinks that Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, are thus dignified here by themselves for this reason, because they were left under marks of infamy by their dying father, Reuben for his incest and Simeon and Levi for their murder of the Shechemites; and therefore Moses would put this particular honour upon them, to magnify God's mercy in their repentance and remission, as a pattern to those that should afterwards believe: the two former seem rather to be mentioned only for the sake of a third, which was Levi, from whom Moses and Aaron descended, and all the priests of the Jewish church. Thus was the tribe of Levi distinguished betimes. Observe here, 1. That Kohath, from whom Moses and Aaron, and all the priests, derived their pedigree, was a younger son of Levi, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.16">v. 16</reference>. Note, The grants of God's favours do not go by seniority of age and priority of birth, but the divine sovereignty often prefers the younger before the elder, so crossing hands. 2. That the ages of Levi, Kohath, and Amram, the father, grandfather, and great grandfather, of Moses, are here recorded; they all lived to a great age, Levi to 137, Kohath to 133, and Amram to 137. Moses himself came much short of them, and fixed seventy or eighty for the ordinary stretch of human life (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Ps. xc. 10</reference>); for now that God's Israel was multiplied and had become a great nation, and divine revelation was by the hand of Moses committed to writing and no longer trusted to tradition, the two great reasons for the long lives of the patriarchs had ceased, and therefore henceforward fewer years must serve men. 3. That Aaron married Elisheba (the same name with that of the wife of Zecharias, Elizabeth, as Miriam is the same with Mary), daughter of Amminadab, one of the chief of the fathers of the tribe of Judah; for the tribes of Levi and Judah often intermarried, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.23">v. 23</reference>. 4. It must not be omitted that Moses has recorded the marriage of his father Amram with Jochebed his own aunt (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.20">v. 20</reference>); and it appears by <reference osisRef="Num.26.59">Num. xxvi. 59</reference> that it must be taken strictly for his father's own sister, at least by the half blood. This marriage was afterwards forbidden as incestuous (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.12">Lev. xviii. 12</reference>), which might be looked upon as a blot upon his family, though before that law; yet Moses does not conceal it, for he sought not his own praise, but wrote with a sincere regard to truth, whether it smiled or frowned upon him. 5. He concludes it with a particular mark of honour on the persons he is writing of, though he himself was one of them, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.26-Exod.6.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. These are <hi type="italic">that Moses and Aaron</hi> whom God pitched upon to be his plenipotentiaries in this treaty. These were those to whom <hi type="italic">God spoke</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.26">v. 26</reference>), and who <hi type="italic">spoke to Pharaoh</hi> on Israel's behalf, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.27">v. 27</reference>. Note, Communion with God and serviceableness to his church are things that, above any other, put true honour upon men. Those are great indeed with whom God converses and whom he employs on his service. Such were that Moses and Aaron; and something of this honour have all his saints, who are made to our God kings and priests. <div eID="gen1562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1563" type="x-p"/> II. In the close of the chapter Moses returns to his narrative, from which he had broken off somewhat abruptly (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">v. 13</reference>), and repeats, 1. The charge God had given him to deliver his message to Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Speak all that I say unto thee,</hi> as a faithful ambassador. Note, Those that go on God's errand must not shun to declare <hi type="italic">the whole counsel of God.</hi> 2. His objection against it, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.30">v. 30</reference>. Note, Those that have at any time spoken unadvisedly with their lips ought often to reflect upon it with regret, as Moses seems to do here.  <chapter eID="Exod.6"/> <div eID="gen1563" type="x-p"/>

entries.afb8ede5f1b31e6d4eba29942244f79f3a5ace20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv632"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.6.1-Exod.6.13">Ex 6:1-13</reference>. Renewal of the Promise.</title> <div sID="gen905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv632"/><hi type="bold">1. the Lord said unto Moses--</hi>The Lord, who is long-suffering and indulgent to the errors and infirmities of His people, made allowance for the mortification of Moses as the result of this first interview and cheered him with the assurance of a speedy and successful termination to his embassy. <div eID="gen905" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff6e428105604e6009efc52f7975f5f0981e6a17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv633"/><div sID="gen906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv633"/><hi type="bold">2. And God spake unto Moses--</hi>For his further encouragement, there was made to him an emphatic repetition of the promise (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.20">Ex 3:20</reference>). <div eID="gen906" type="x-p"/>
entries.4987a777f6b5af7003a8ac7f62bd58ae0b0ef2e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv634"/><div sID="gen907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv634"/><hi type="bold">3. I ... God Almighty--</hi>All enemies must fall, all difficulties must vanish before My omnipotent power, and the patriarchs had abundant proofs of this.<div eID="gen907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but by my name, &c.--</hi>rather, interrogatively, by My name Jehovah was I not known to them? Am not I, the Almighty God, who pledged My honor for the fulfilment of the covenant, also the self-existent God who lives to accomplish it? Rest assured, therefore, that I shall bring it to pass. This passage has occasioned much discussion; and it has been thought by many to intimate that as the name Jehovah was not known to the patriarchs, at least in the full bearing or practical experience of it, the honor of the disclosure was reserved to Moses, who was the first sent with a message in the name of Jehovah, and enabled to attest it by a series of public miracles. <div eID="gen908" type="x-p"/>
entries.590ae9ce7dccbc2005631789668c157d24b72543: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv635"/><div sID="gen909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv635"/><hi type="bold">9-11. Moses spake so unto the children of Israel--</hi>The increased severities inflicted on the Israelites seem to have so entirely crushed their spirits, as well as irritated them, that they refused to listen to any more communications (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.12">Ex 14:12</reference>). Even the faith of Moses himself was faltering; and he would have abandoned the enterprise in despair had he not received a positive command from God to revisit the people without delay, and at the same time renew their demand on the king in a more decisive and peremptory tone. <div eID="gen909" type="x-p"/>
entries.215c5c23f9606760694ff330df92d780b37aee5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv636"/><div sID="gen910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv636"/><hi type="bold">12. how then shall ... who am of uncircumcised lips?--</hi>A metaphorical expression among the Hebrews, who, taught to look on the circumcision of any part as denoting perfection, signified its deficiency or unsuitableness by uncircumcision. The words here express how painfully Moses felt his want of utterance or persuasive oratory. He seems to have fallen into the same deep despondency as his brethren, and to be shrinking with nervous timidity from a difficult, if not desperate, cause. If he had succeeded so ill with the people, whose dearest interests were all involved, what better hope could he entertain of his making more impression on the heart of a king elated with pride and strong in the possession of absolute power? How strikingly was the indulgent forbearance of God displayed towards His people amid all their backwardness to hail His announcement of approaching deliverance! No perverse complaints or careless indifference on their part retarded the development of His gracious purposes. On the contrary, here, as generally, the course of His providence is slow in the infliction of judgments, while it moves more quickly, as it were, when misery is to be relieved or benefits conferred. <div eID="gen910" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebf11565423b43b29f87dfc548105d25ed0e4881: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv637"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.6.14-Exod.6.30">Ex 6:14-30</reference>. The Genealogy of Moses.</title> <div sID="gen911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv637"/><hi type="bold">14-15. These be the heads of their fathers' houses--</hi>chiefs or governors of their houses. The insertion of this genealogical table in this part of the narrative was intended to authenticate the descent of Moses and Aaron. Both of them were commissioned to act so important a part in the events transacted in the court of Egypt and afterwards elevated to so high offices in the government and Church of God, that it was of the utmost importance that their lineage should be accurately traced. Reuben and Simeon being the oldest of Jacob's sons, a passing notice is taken of them, and then the historian advances to the enumeration of the principal persons in the house of Levi [Ex 6:16-19]. <div eID="gen911" type="x-p"/>
entries.720def6b69c57d135906fd78804e0f722b28124d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv638"/><div sID="gen912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv638"/><hi type="bold">20. Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife--</hi>The Septuagint and Syriac versions render it "his cousin." <div eID="gen912" type="x-p"/>
entries.03f6d5f23439fb6a6176a8e4f818a66bbc4e39f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv639"/><div sID="gen913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv639"/><hi type="bold">23. Elisheba--</hi>that is, Elizabethan. These minute particulars recorded of the family of Aaron, while he has passed over his own, indicate the real modesty of Moses. An ambitious man or an impostor would have acted in a different manner. <chapter eID="Exod.6"/>

entries.34cd19b4c96a2914602e44c0f07f1f3d2987e7a9: <div eID="gen2517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen2518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> God encourages Moses, and promises to show wonders upon Pharaoh, and to bring out his people with a strong hand, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.1">Exo 6:1</reference>. He confirms this promise by his essential name Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.2">Exo 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>; by the covenant he had made with their fathers, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.4">Exo 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.5">Exo 6:5</reference>. Sends Moses with a fresh message to the Hebrews, full of the most gracious promises, and confirms the whole by appealing to the name in which his unchangeable existence is implied, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.6-Exo.6.8">Exo 6:6-8</reference>. Moses delivers the message to the Israelites, but through anguish of spirit they do not believe, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.9">Exo 6:9</reference>. He receives a new commission to go to Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.10">Exo 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.11">Exo 6:11</reference>. He excuses himself on account of his unreadiness of speech, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>. The Lord gives him and Aaron a charge both to Pharaoh and to the children of Israel, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.13">Exo 6:13</reference>. The genealogy of Reuben, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.14">Exo 6:14</reference>; of Simeon, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.15">Exo 6:15</reference>; of Levi, from whom descended Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.16">Exo 6:16</reference>. The sons of Gershon, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.17">Exo 6:17</reference>; of Kohath, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.15">Exo 6:15</reference>; of Merari, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.19">Exo 6:19</reference>. The marriage of Amram and Jochebed, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.20">Exo 6:20</reference>. The sons of Izhar and Uzziel, the brothers of Amram, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.21">Exo 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.22">Exo 6:22</reference>. Marriage of Aaron and Elisheba, and the birth of their sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.23">Exo 6:23</reference>. The sons of Korah, the nephew of Aaron, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.24">Exo 6:24</reference>. The marriage of Eleazar to one of the daughters of Putiel, and the birth of Phinehas, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.25">Exo 6:25</reference>. These genealogical accounts introduced for the sake of showing the line of descent of Moses and Aaron, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.26">Exo 6:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.27">Exo 6:27</reference>. A recapitulation of the commission delivered to Moses and Aaron, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.29">Exo 6:29</reference>, and a repetition of the excuse formerly made by Moses, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.30">Exo 6:30</reference>. <div eID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> With a strong hand - יד חזקה yad chazakah, the same verb which we translate to harden; see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.4.21">Exo 4:21</reference> (note). The strong hand here means sovereign power, suddenly and forcibly applied. God purposed to manifest his sovereign power in the sight of Pharaoh and the Egyptians; in consequence of which Pharaoh would manifest his power and authority as sovereign of Egypt, in dismissing and thrusting out the people. See <reference osisRef="Exo.12.31-Exo.12.33">Exo 12:31-33</reference>.
entries.cbf35183aa532569859969fa8d6e991b252d6968: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> I am the Lord - It should be, I am Jehovah, and without this the reason of what is said in the 3d verse is not sufficiently obvious.
entries.2f24729384b250719fe05e2e49900b4518f0ab33: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> By the name of God Almighty - אל שדי EL-Shaddal, God All-sufficient; God the dispenser or pourer-out of gifts. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Gen 17:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> But by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them - This passage has been a sort of crux criticorum, and has been variously explained. It is certain that the name Jehovah was in use long before the days of Abraham, see <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference>, where the words יהוה אלהים Jehovah Elohim occur, as they do frequently afterwards; and see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">Gen 15:2</reference>, where Abraham expressly addresses him by the name Adonai Jehovah; and see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7">Gen 15:7</reference>, where God reveals himself to Abraham by this very name: And he said unto him, I am Jehovah, that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees. How then can it be said that by his name Jehovah he was not known unto them? Several answers have been given to this question; the following are the chief: - 1. The words should be read interrogatively, for the negative particle לא lo, not, has this power often in Hebrew. "I appeared unto Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by the name of God Almighty, and by my name Jehovah was I not also made known unto them?" 2. The name Jehovah was not revealed before the time mentioned here, for though it occurs so frequently in the book of Genesis, as that book was written long after the name had come into common use, as a principal characteristic of God, Moses employs it in his history because of this circumstance; so that whenever it appears previously to this, it is by the figure called prolepsis or anticipation. 3. As the name יהוה Jehovah signifies existence, it may be understood in the text in question thus: "I appeared unto Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by my name God Almighty, or God All-sufficient, i.e., having all power to do all good; in this character I made a covenant with them, supported by great and glorious promises; but as those promises had respect unto their posterity, they could not be fulfilled to those fathers: but now, as Jehovah, I am about to give existence to all those promises relative to your support, deliverance from bondage, and your consequent settlement in the promised land." 4. The words may be considered as used comparatively: though God did appear to those patriarchs as Jehovah, and they acknowledged him by this name, yet it was but comparatively known unto them; they knew nothing of the power and goodness of God, in comparison of what the Israelites were now about to experience. <div eID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> I believe the simple meaning is this, that though from the beginning the name Jehovah was known as one of the names of the Supreme Being, yet what it really implied they did not know. אל שלי El-Shaddai, God All-sufficient, they knew well by the continual provision he made for them, and the constant protection he afforded them: but the name יהוה Jehovah is particularly to be referred to the accomplishment of promises already made; to the giving them a being, and thus bringing them into existence, which could not have been done in the order of his providence sooner than here specified: this name therefore in its power and significancy was not known unto them; nor fully known unto their descendants till the deliverance from Egypt and the settlement in the promised land. It is surely possible for a man to bear the name of a certain office or dignity before he fulfills any of its functions. King, mayor, alderman, magistrate, constable, may be borne by the several persons to whom they legally belong, before any of the acts peculiar to those offices are performed. The King, acknowledged as such on his coronation, is known to be such by his legislative acts; the civil magistrate, by his distribution of justice, and issuing warrants for the apprehending of culprits; and the constable, by executing those warrants. All these were known to have their respective names, but the exercise of their powers alone shows what is implied in being king, magistrate, and constable. The following is a case in point, which fell within my own knowledge. <div eID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> A case of dispute between certain litigious neighbors being heard in court before a weekly sitting of the magistrates, a woman who came as an evidence in behalf of her bad neighbor, finding the magistrates inclining to give judgment against her mischievous companion, took her by the arm and said, "Come away! I told you you would get neither law nor justice in this place." A magistrate, who was as much an honor to his function as he was to human nature, immediately said, "Here, constable! take that woman and lodge her in Bridewell, that she may know there is some law and justice in this place." Thus the worthy magistrate proved he had the power implied in the name by executing the duties of his office. And God who was known as Jehovah, the being who makes and gives effect to promises, was known to the descendants of the twelve tribes to be That Jehovah, by giving effect and being to the promises which he had made to their fathers.
entries.5366322b438b8e219adbed046bd0713b55bb0aa7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> I have also established my covenant - I have now fully purposed to give present effect to all my engagements with your fathers, in behalf of their posterity.
entries.3ed1cc6eb963f6c1106e9f6c708cc166fad57bbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2529" type="x-p"/> Say unto the children of Israel, I am the Lord, and I will bring you out, etc. - This confirms the explanation given of <reference osisRef="Exo.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>, which see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>.
entries.3df50768392faace9a8815b4ab5e466653c922df: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen2529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2530" type="x-p"/> I will take you to me for a people, etc. - This was precisely the covenant that he had made with Abraham. See <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen 17:7</reference>, and see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen 17:7</reference>. <div eID="gen2530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2531" type="x-p"/> And ye shall know that I am the Lord your God - By thus fulfilling my promises ye shall know what is implied in my name. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>. <div eID="gen2531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2532" type="x-p"/> But why should God take such a most stupid, refractory, and totally worthless people for his people? 1. Because he had promised to do so to their noble ancestors Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Judah, etc., men worthy of all praise, because in general friends of God, devoted to his will and to the good of mankind. <div eID="gen2532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2533" type="x-p"/> 2. "That (as Bishop Warburton properly observes) the extraordinary providence by which they were protected, might become the more visible and illustrious; for had they been endowed with the shining qualities of the more polished nations, the effects of that providence might have been ascribed to their own wisdom." <div eID="gen2533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2534" type="x-p"/> 3. That God might show to all succeeding generations that he delights to instruct the ignorant, help the weak, and save the lost; for if he bore long with Israel, showed them especial mercy, and graciously received them whenever they implored his protection, none need despair. God seems to have chosen the worst people in the universe, to give by them unto mankind the highest and most expressive proofs, that he wills not the death of a sinner, but rather that he may turn from his iniquity and live.
entries.5ab525f7615fec70bd6e87cd08f62e01cf10597e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen2534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2535" type="x-p"/> Which I did swear - נשאתי את ידי nasathi eth yadi, I have lifted up my hand. The usual mode of making an appeal to God, and hence considered to be a form of swearing. It is thus that <reference osisRef="Isa.62.8">Isa 62:8</reference> is to be understood: The Lord hath sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength.
entries.2580238fc608a686373bd8ebc9aae8ebc868f54c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen2535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2536" type="x-p"/> But they hearkened not - Their bondage was become so extremely oppressive that they had lost all hope of ever being redeemed from it. After this verse the Samaritan adds, Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians: for it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than that we should die in the wilderness. This appears to be borrowed from <reference osisRef="Exo.14.12">Exo 14:12</reference>. <div eID="gen2536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2537" type="x-p"/> Anguish of spirit - קצר רוח kotzer ruach, shortness of spirit or breath. The words signify that their labor was so continual, and their bondage so cruel and oppressive, that they had scarcely time to breathe.
entries.a036cde6b1a3b1247ed5c9d42f4f0d8a4545c50f: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen2537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2538" type="x-p"/> Uncircumcised lips? - The word ערל aral, which we translate uncircumcised, seems to signify any thing exuberant or superfluous. Had not Moses been remarkable for his excellent beauty, I should have thought the passage might be rendered protuberant lips; but as this sense cannot be admitted for the above reason, the word must refer to some natural impediment in his speech; and probably means a want of distinct and ready utterance, either occasioned by some defect in the organs of speech, or impaired knowledge of the Egyptian language after an absence of forty years. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.4.10">Exo 4:10</reference>.
entries.e75e7776ed1c0d0b91f048a37af16a1d9b214b76: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen2538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2539" type="x-p"/> These be the heads - ראשי rashey, the chiefs or captains. The following genealogy was simply intended to show that Moses and Aaron came in a direct line from Abraham, and to ascertain the time of Israel's deliverance. The whole account from <reference osisRef="Exo.6.14-Exo.6.26">Exo 6:14-26</reference> inclusive, is a sort of parenthesis, and does not belong to the narration; and what follows from <reference osisRef="Exo.6.28">Exo 6:28</reference> is a recapitulation of what was spoken in the preceding chapters.
entries.cee0d5d1b5c9b016c911ba937fcfa17fd7eee6fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen2539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2540" type="x-p"/> The years of the life of Levi - "Bishop Patrick observes that Levi is thought to have lived the longest of all Jacob's sons, none of whose ages are recorded in Scripture but his and Joseph's, whom Levi survived twenty-seven years, though he was much the elder brother. By the common computation this would be twenty-three years: by Kennicott's computation at the end of Genesis 31. (See Clarke's note at <reference osisRef="Gen.31.55">Gen 31:55</reference>) Levi's birth is placed twenty-four years before that of Joseph; his death, therefore, would be only three years later. But this is not the only difficulty in ancient chronologies. Kohath, the second son of Levi, according to Archbishop Usher was thirty years old when Jacob came into Egypt, and lived there one hundred and three years. He attained to nearly the same age with Levi, to one hundred and thirty-three years; and his son Amram, the father of Moses, lived to the same age with Levi. We may observe here how the Divine promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen 15:16</reference>, of delivering the Israelites out of Egypt in the fourth generation was verified; for Moses was the son of Amram, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, the son of Jacob." - Dodd.
entries.04a72b2e3797ad9f417a27bd741560a7b8fca6fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen2540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2541" type="x-p"/> His father's sister - דדתו dodatho. The true meaning of this word is uncertain. Parkhurst observes that דוד dod signifies an uncle in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.14">1Sam 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.4">Lev 10:4</reference>, and frequently elsewhere. It signifies also an uncle's son, a cousin-german: compare <reference osisRef="Jer.32.8">Jer 32:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Exo.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>, where the Vulgate renders דדי dodi by patruelis mei, my paternal cousin; and in <reference osisRef="Amo.6.10">Amo 6:10</reference>, for דודו dodo, the Targum has קריביה karibiah, his near relation. So the Vulgate, propinquus ejus, his relative, and the Septuagint, οἱ οικειοι αυτων, those of their household. The best critics suppose that Jochebed was the cousin-german of Amram, and not his aunt. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.2.1">Exo 2:1</reference>. <div eID="gen2541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2542" type="x-p"/> Bare him Aaron and Moses - The Samaritan, Septuagint, Syriac, and one Hebrew MS. add, And Miriam their sister. Some of the best critics suppose these words to have been originally in the Hebrew text.
entries.f692de2e1b86d4c42cd51c8ea48088b281735f2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen2542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2543" type="x-p"/> Korah - Though he became a rebel against God and Moses, (see <reference osisRef="Num.16.1">Num 16:1</reference>, etc)., yet Moses, in his great impartiality, inserts his name among those of his other progenitors.
entries.9a585af11b10a83b31fec2ac8347f11a5273f4be: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen2543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2544" type="x-p"/> Uzziel - He is called Aaron's uncle, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.4">Lev 10:4</reference>.
entries.0e97eaa7712586d7db253464502a311c4914ba48: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen2544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2545" type="x-p"/> Elisheba - The oath of the Lord. It is the same name as Elizabeth, so very common among Christians. She was of the royal tribe of Judah, and was sister to Nahshon, one of the princes; see <reference osisRef="Num.2.3">Num 2:3</reference>. <div eID="gen2545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2546" type="x-p"/> Eleazar - He succeeded to the high priesthood on the death of his father Aaron, <reference osisRef="Num.20.25">Num 20:25</reference>, etc.
entries.27429ee40bec98f65eb93c4fefc88dd640730dde: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen2546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2547" type="x-p"/> Phinehas - Of the celebrated act of this person, and the most honorable grant made to him and his posterity, see <reference osisRef="Num.25.7-Num.25.13">Num 25:7-13</reference>.
entries.7ba0c7500f48d843cd5f9a58c711aeb09e6c5172: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen2547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2548" type="x-p"/> According to their armies - צבאתם tsibotham, their battalions - regularly arranged troops. As God had these particularly under his care and direction, he had the name of יהוה צבאות Yehovah tsebaoth, Lord of hosts or armies. "The plain and disinterested manner," says Dr. Dodd, "in which Moses speaks here of his relations, and the impartiality wherewith he inserts in the list of them such as were afterwards severely punished by the Lord, are striking proofs of his modesty and sincerity. He inserts the genealogy of Reuben and Simeon, because they were of the same mother with Levi; and though he says nothing of himself, yet he relates particularly what concerns Aaron, <reference osisRef="Exo.6.23">Exo 6:23</reference>, who married into an honorable family, the sister of a prince of the tribe of Judah."
entries.a752e0c202c0338b85a43c3acf7c5b61d16d9e60: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen2548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2549" type="x-p"/> And it came to pass - Here the seventh chapter should commence, as there is a complete ending of the sixth with <reference osisRef="Exo.6.27">Exo 6:27</reference>, and the <reference osisRef="Exo.6.30">Exo 6:30</reference> of this chapter is intimately connected with the 1st verse of the succeeding. <div eID="gen2549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2550" type="x-p"/> The principal subjects in this chapter have been so amply considered in the notes, that little of importance remains to be done. On the nature of a covenant (See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.6.4">Exo 6:4</reference>). ample information may be obtained by referring to <reference osisRef="Gen.6.18">Gen 6:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9-Gen.15.18">Gen 15:9-18</reference>, which places the reader will do well to consult. <div eID="gen2550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2551" type="x-p"/> Supposing Moses to have really labored under some defect in speech, we may consider it as wisely designed to be a sort of counterbalance to his other excellences: at least this is an ordinary procedure of Divine Providence; personal accomplishments are counterbalanced by mental defects, and mental imperfections often by personal accomplishments. Thus the head cannot say to the foot, I have no need of thee. And God does all this in great wisdom, to hide pride from man, and that no flesh may glory in his presence. To be contented with our formation, endowments, and external circumstances, requires not only much submission to the providence of God, but also much of the mind of Christ. On the other hand, should we feel vanity because of some personal or mental accomplishment, we have only to take a view of our whole to find sufficient cause of humiliation; and after all, the meek and gentle spirit only is, in the sight of God, of great price.  <chapter eID="Exod.6"/> <div eID="gen2551" type="x-p"/>

entries.62a985d2086ed838cd74f33b860342470f3f2577: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.1-Exod.6.6">Exo 6:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen689" type="x-p"/> Equipment of Moses and Aaron as Messengers of Jehovah. - Exo 6:1. In reply to the complaining inquiry of Moses, <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> promised him the deliverance of Israel by a strong hand (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.3.19">Exo 3:19</reference>), by which Pharaoh would be compelled to let Israel go, and even to drive them out of his land. Moses did not receive any direct answer to the question, “Why hast Thou so evil-entreated this people?” He was to gather this first of all from his own experience as the leader of Israel. For the words were strictly applicable here: “What I do thou knowest not now, but thou shalt know hereafter” (Joh 13:7). If, even after the miraculous deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt and their glorious march through the desert, in which they had received so many proofs of the omnipotence and mercy of their God, they repeatedly rebelled against the guidance of God, and were not content with the manna provided by the Lord, but lusted after the fishes, leeks, and onions of Egypt (Num 11); ); it is certain that in such a state of mind as this, they would never have been willing to leave Egypt and enter into a covenant with Jehovah, without a very great increase in the oppression they endured in Egypt. - The brief but comprehensive promise was still further explained by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.2-Exod.6.9">Exo 6:2-9</reference>), and Moses was instructed and authorized to carry out the divine purposes in concert with Aaron (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.10-Exod.6.13">Exo 6:10-13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.28-Exod.6.30">Exo 6:28-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.7.1-Exod.7.6">Exo 7:1-6</reference>). The genealogy of the two messengers is then introduced into the midst of these instructions (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.14-Exod.6.27">Exo 6:14-27</reference>); and the age of Moses is given at the close (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.7">Exo 7:7</reference>). This section does not contain a different account of the calling of Moses, taken from some other source than the previous one; it rather presupposes <reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Exo 3-5</reference>, and completes the account commenced in Exo 3 of the equipment of Moses and Aaron as the executors of the divine will with regard to Pharaoh and Israel. For the fact that the first visit paid by Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh was simply intended to bring out the attitude of Pharaoh towards the purposes of Jehovah, and to show the necessity for the great judgments of God, is distinctly expressed in the words, “Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh.” But before these judgments commenced, Jehovah announced to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.2">Exo 6:2</reference>), and through him to the people, that henceforth He would manifest Himself to them in a much more glorious manner than to the patriarchs, namely, as Jehovah; whereas to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, He had only appeared as El Shaddai. The words, “By My name Jehovah was I now known to them,” do not mean, however, that the patriarchs were altogether ignorant of the name Jehovah. This is obvious from the significant use of that name, which was not an unmeaning sound, but a real expression of the divine nature, and still more from the unmistakeable connection between the explanation given by God here and Gen 17:1. When the establishment of the covenant commenced, as described in Gen 15, with the institution of the covenant sign of circumcision and the promise of the birth of Isaac, Jehovah said to Abram, “I am El Shaddai, God Almighty,” and from that time forward manifested Himself to Abram and his wife as the Almighty, in the birth of Isaac, which took place apart altogether from the powers of nature, and also in the preservation, guidance, and multiplication of his seed. It was in His attribute as El Shaddai that God had revealed His nature to the patriarchs; but now He was about to reveal Himself to Israel as Jehovah, as the absolute Being working with unbounded freedom in the performance of His promises. For not only had He established His covenant with the fathers (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.4">Exo 6:4</reference>), but He had also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, and remembered His covenant (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.5">Exo 6:5</reference>; וגם - וגם, not only - but also). The divine promise not only commences in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.2">Exo 6:2</reference>, but concludes at <reference osisRef="Exod.6.8">Exo 6:8</reference>, with the emphatic expression, “<hi type="italic">I</hi> Jehovah,” to show that the work of Israel’s redemption resided in the power of the name Jehovah. In <reference osisRef="Exod.6.4">Exo 6:4</reference> the covenant promises of <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7-Gen.17.8">Gen 17:7-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.3">Gen 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.11-Gen.35.12">Gen 35:11-12</reference>, are all brought together; and in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.5">Exo 6:5</reference> we have a repetition of <reference osisRef="Exod.2.24">Exo 2:24</reference>, with the emphatically repeated אני (<hi type="italic">I</hi>). On the ground of the erection of His covenant on the one hand, and, what was irreconcilable with that covenant, the bondage of Israel on the other, Jehovah was not about to redeem Israel from its sufferings and make it His own nation. This assurance, which God would carry out by the manifestation of His nature as expressed in the name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, contained three distinct elements: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) the deliverance of Israel from the bondage of Egypt, which, because so utterly different from all outward appearances, is described in three parallel clauses: bringing them out from under the burdens of the Egyptians; saving them from their bondage; and redeeming them with a stretched-out arm and with great judgments; - (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) the adoption of Israel as the nation of God; - (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) the guidance of Israel into the land promised to the fathers (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.6-Exod.6.8">Exo 6:6-8</reference>). נטוּיה זרוע, a stretched-out arm, is most appropriately connected with גּדלים שׁפטים, great judgments; for God raises, stretches out His arm, when He proceeds in judgment to smite the rebellious. These expressions repeat with greater emphasis the “strong hand” of <reference osisRef="Exod.6.1">Exo 6:1</reference>, and are frequently connected with it in the rhetorical language of Deuteronomy (e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">Deu 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.19">Deu 7:19</reference>). The “great judgments” were the plagues, the judgments of God, by which Pharaoh was to be compelled to let Israel go.
entries.f4939cf8a8faed566325ca82a52ac3212ecd6b0c: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.7-Exod.6.8">Exo 6:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen690" type="x-p"/> The adoption of Israel as the nation of God took place at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exo 19:5</reference>). וגו נשׁאתי אשׁר, “<hi type="italic">with regard to which I have lifted up My hand to give it</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.8">Exo 6:8</reference>). Lifting up the hand (sc., towards heaven) is the attitude of swearing (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.40">Deu 32:40</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.14.22">Gen 14:22</reference>); and these words point back to Gen 22:16. and <reference osisRef="Gen.26.3">Gen 26:3</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.24.7">Gen 24:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.50.24">Gen 50:24</reference>).
entries.79edf3e05235c8347e1b6bdd53f3ca7725681f22: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.9-Exod.6.12">Exo 6:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen691" type="x-p"/> When Moses communicated this solemn assurance of God to the people, they did not listen to him רוּה מּקּצר, lit., “<hi type="italic">for shortness of breath;</hi>” not “from impatience” (like קצר־רוּח, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.29">Pro 14:29</reference>, in contrast to אפּים ארך), but from anguish, inward pressure, which prevents a man from breathing properly. Thus the early belief of the Israelites was changed into the despondency of unbelief through the increase of their oppression. This result also produced despondency in Moses’ mind, so that he once more declined the commission, which followed the promise, viz., to go to Pharaoh and demand that he would let Israel go out of his land (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.11">Exo 6:11</reference>). If the children of Israel would not listen to him, how should Pharaoh hear him, especially as he was uncircumcised in the lips (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>)? שׁפתים ערל is one whose lips are, as it were, covered with a foreskin, so that he cannot easily bring out his words; in meaning the same as “heavy of mouth” in Exo 4:10. The reply of God to this objection is given in <reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exo 7:1</reference>-5. For, before the historian gives the decisive answer of Jehovah which removed all further hesitation on the part of Moses, and completed his mission and that of Aaron to Pharaoh, he considers it advisable to introduce the genealogy of the two men of God, for the purpose of showing clearly their genealogical relation to the people of Israel.
entries.be1ba5e2ce1e69dc63e63213ce5df0472aff6351: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">Exo 6:13</reference> <div eID="gen691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen692" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Exod.6.13">Exo 6:13</reference> forms a concluding summary, and prepares the way for the genealogy that follows, the heading of which is given in Exo 6:14.<note placement="foot">The organic connection of this genealogy with the entire narrative has been so conclusively demonstrated by <hi type="italic">Ranke</hi>, in his <hi type="italic">Unterss. ub. d. Pent</hi>. i. p. 68ff. and ii. 19ff., that even <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> has admitted it, and thrown away the fragmentary hypothesis.</note>
entries.8863398d5bd8f86111a2f1c425591bc51eadc1bd: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.14-Exod.6.27">Exo 6:14-27</reference> <div eID="gen692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen693" type="x-p"/> The Genealogy of Moses and Aaron. - “<hi type="italic">These are their</hi> (Moses’ and Aaron’s) <hi type="italic">father's-houses</hi>.” בּית־אבות father's-houses (not fathers’ house) is a composite noun, so formed that the two words not only denote one idea, but are treated grammatically as one word, like בּית־עצבּים idol-houses (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.9">1Sa 31:9</reference>), and בּית־בּמות high-place-houses (cf. <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §108, 3; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §270 <hi type="italic">c</hi>). <hi type="italic">Father’s house</hi> was a technical term applied to a collection of families, called by the name of a common ancestor. The father's-houses were the larger divisions into which the families (<hi type="italic">mishpachoth</hi>), the largest subdivisions of the tribes of Israel, were grouped. To show clearly the genealogical position of Levi, the tribe-father of Moses and Aaron, among the sons of Jacob, the genealogy commences with Reuben, the first-born of Jacob, and gives the names of such of his sons and those of Simeon as were the founders of families (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.9-Gen.46.10">Gen 46:9-10</reference>). Then follows Levi; and not only are the names of his three sons given, but the length of his life is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.16">Exo 6:16</reference>), also that of his son Kohath and his descendant Amram, because they were the tribe-fathers of Moses and Aaron. But the Amram mentioned in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.20">Exo 6:20</reference> as the father of Moses, cannot be the same person as the Amram who was the son of Kohath (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.18">Exo 6:18</reference>), but must be a later descendant. For, however the sameness of names may seem to favour the identity of the persons, if we simply look at the genealogy before us, a comparison of this passage with Num 3:27-28 will show the impossibility of such an assumption. “According to Num 3:27-28, the Kohathites were divided (in Moses’ time) into the four branches, Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites, who consisted together of 8600 men and boys (women and girls not being included). Of these, about a fourth, or 2150 men, would belong to the Amramites. Now, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.18.3-Exod.18.4">Exo 18:3-4</reference>, Moses himself had only two sons. Consequently, if Amram the son of Kohath, and tribe-father of the Amramites, was the same person as Amram the father of Moses, Moses must have had 2147 brothers and brothers’ sons (the brothers’ daughters, the sisters, and their daughters, not being reckoned at all). But as this is absolutely impossible, it must be granted that Amram the son of Kohath was not the father of Moses, and that an indefinitely long list of generations has been omitted between the former and his descendant of the same name” (Tiele, Chr. des A. T. p. 36).<note placement="foot">The objections of <hi type="italic">M. Baumgarten</hi> to these correct remarks have been conclusively met by <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> (Hist. of O. C. vol. ii. p. 144). We find a similar case in the genealogy of Ezra in Ezr 7:3, which passes over from Azariah the son of Meraioth to Azariah the son of Johanan, and omits five links between the two, as we may see from <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.7">1Ch 6:7</reference>-11. In the same way the genealogy before us skips over from Amram the son of Kohath to Amram the father of Moses without mentioning the generations between.</note> <div eID="gen693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen694" type="x-p"/> The enumeration of only four generations, viz., Levi, Iohath, Amram, Moses, is unmistakeably related to <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen 15:16</reference>, where it is stated that the fourth generation would return to Canaan. Amram’s wife <hi type="italic">Jochebed</hi>, who is merely spoken of in general terms as a daughter of Levi (a Levitess) in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.1">Exo 2:1</reference> and Num 26:59, is called here the דּודה “<hi type="italic">aunt</hi>” (father’s sister) of Amram, a marriage which was prohibited in the Mosaic law (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.12">Lev 18:12</reference>), but was allowed before the giving of the law; so that there is no reason for following the lxx and <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>, and rendering the word, in direct opposition to the usage of the language, <hi type="italic">patruelis</hi>, the father’s brother’s daughter. Amram’s sons are placed according to their age: Aaron, then Moses, as Aaron was three years older than his brother. Their sister Miriam was older still (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.2.4">Exo 2:4</reference>). In the lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>., and one Hebrew MS, she is mentioned here; but this is a later interpolation. In Exo 6:21. not only are the sons of Aaron mentioned (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.23">Exo 6:23</reference>), but those of two of Amram’s brothers, Izhar and Uzziel (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.21">Exo 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.22">Exo 6:22</reference>), and also Phinehas, the son of Aaron’s son Eleazar (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.25">Exo 6:25</reference>); as the genealogy was intended to trace the descent of the principal priestly families, among which again special prominence is given to Aaron and Eleazar by the introduction of their wives. On the other hand, none of the sons of Moses are mentioned, because his dignity was limited to his own person, and his descendants fell behind those of Aaron, and were simply reckoned among the non-priestly families of Levi. The Korahites and Uzzielites are mentioned, but a superior rank was assigned to them in the subsequent history to that of other Levitical families (cf. Num 16-17; Num 26:11, and Num 3:30 with <reference osisRef="Lev.10.4">Lev 10:4</reference>). Aaron’s wife <hi type="italic">Elisheba</hi> was of the princely tribe of Judah, and her brother Naashon was a tribe-prince of Judah (cf. Num 2:3). אבות ראשׁי (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.25">Exo 6:25</reference>), a frequent abbreviation for בית־אבות ראשׁי, heads of the father's-houses of the Levites. In <reference osisRef="Exod.6.26">Exo 6:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.6.27">Exo 6:27</reference>, with which the genealogy closes, the object of introducing it is very clearly shown in the expression, “<hi type="italic">These are that Aaron and Moses,</hi>” at the beginning of <reference osisRef="Exod.6.26">Exo 6:26</reference>; and again, “<hi type="italic">These are that Moses and Aaron,</hi>” at the close of Exo 6:27. The reversal of the order of the names is also to be noticed. In the genealogy itself Aaron stands first, as the elder of the two; in the conclusion, which leads over to the historical narrative that follows, Moses takes precedence of his elder brother, as being the divinely appointed redeemer of Israel. On the expression, “according to their armies,” see Exo 7:4.
entries.0b5ea52e8e43305a04e9c35755ea1caa80350497: <reference osisRef="Exod.6.28-Exod.6.30">Exo 6:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen695" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Exod.6.28-Exod.6.30">Exo 6:28-30</reference> the thread of the history, which was broken off at <reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>, is again resumed. דּבּר בּיום, on the day, i.e., at the time, when God spake. יום is the construct state before an entire clause, which is governed by it without a relative particle, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.35">Lev 7:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.15">1Sa 25:15</reference> (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §286 <hi type="italic">i</hi>).  <chapter eID="Exod.6"/> <div eID="gen695" type="x-p"/>

entries.4a0b84559c1be6388488cf612992beb277251c8d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Exod.6.1" sID="gen6891" type="section"/> <div sID="gen6892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Then the Lord said unto Moses.</hi> Moses was indeed unworthy of receiving so kind and gentle a reply from God; but the Father of all goodness of His infinite mercy pardoned both the sins of Moses and of the people, that He might effect the deliverance which he had determined. Yet He adduces nothing new, but repeats and confirms His former declaration, that Pharaoh would not obey until forcibly compelled to do so. The expression, “thou shalt see,” is a tacit reproof of his immoderate impatience, in not waiting for the result of the promise. The reason is then added why God is unwilling that His people should be spontaneously dismissed by the tyrant, viz., because He wished the work of their liberation to be conspicuous. We must remark the strength of the words “drive them out;” as if He had said, that when Pharaoh had been subdued, and routed in the contest, he would not only consent, but would consider it a great blessing, for the people to depart as quickly as possible. The sum is, that he, who today refuses to let you depart, will not only set you free, but will even expel you from his kingdom.<div eID="gen6892" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen6891" osisID="Exod.6.1" type="section"/>
entries.0f5e960bd4b1669171da957fb0bfc92bb7f6b218: <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Exod.6.2" sID="gen6893" type="section"/> <div sID="gen6894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And God spake.</hi> God pursues His address, that Moses may again uplift the fainting courage of the people. Moreover, He rebukes their distrust, by recalling the memory of His covenant; for if this had been duly impressed upon their minds, they would have been much more firm in their expectation of deliverance. He therefore shews that He has now advanced nothing new; since they had heard long ago from the Patriarchs that they were chosen by God as His peculiar people, and had almost imbibed from their mother’s breasts the doctrine of his adoption of them. Wherefore their stupidity is the more unpardonable, and more manifest, when they thus factiously complain of Moses, as if he had himself invented what he had promised them in the name of God. He also stings them by an implied comparison; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had eagerly embraced the promise given them, and had quietly, and perseveringly trusted in it; whilst they, who boasted of their descent from that holy stock, disdainfully rejected it, because its fulfillment did not immediately appear. And, in order to amplify their sin, he reasons from the less to the greater: since a fuller and clearer manifestation of it is presented to them than there had been to the fathers, it follows that they ought to have been more ready to believe it. Whence it is plain that their stupidity is inexcusable, since they will not receive God, when he is so familiarly presenting himself to them. Translators do not agree as to the epithet “Sadai.” Some derive it from the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שדד</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shadad</hi>, and imagine that the final letter <foreign xml:lang="he">י</foreign>, <hi type="italic">yod</hi>, is the double <foreign xml:lang="he">ד</foreign>, <hi type="italic">daleth</hi> If we agree to this, it will mean the same as “the Destroyer;” or at any rate will signify the awful majesty of God. Others are rather of opinion that the root is <foreign xml:lang="he">שד</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shad</hi>, which means “a teat.” To others it appears to be a compound word from the relative <foreign xml:lang="he">אשר</foreign>, <hi type="italic">esher</hi>, or <foreign xml:lang="he">ש</foreign>, and <foreign xml:lang="he">די</foreign>, <hi type="italic">di</hi>, which in Hebrew means “<hi type="italic">sufficiency</hi>.” Thus he will be called “Sadai,” who abounds with all good things. It is indeed sure that they use this word in a good as well as a bad sense; for where Isaiah threatens that God will be the avenger of sins, he calls him “Sadai.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.9">Isaiah 13:9</reference>.) So also in <reference osisRef="Bible:Job.23.16">Job 23:16</reference>, “Sadai troubleth me.” In these and similar passages, the terrible power of God is unquestionably expressed; but when He promises to Abraham that He will be the God “Sadai,” He is engaging himself to be merciful and bounteous. Here again, where He says that He appeared to the Fathers as the God “Sadai,” He has not respect so much to His might in exercising judgment, as to His abundant and perfect loving-kindness; as though He had said, that He had manifested to Abraham and the other Patriarchs how great was His efficiency in preserving and defending His own people, and that they had known from experience how powerfully and effectually He cherishes, sustains, and aids them that are His. But although He declares what benefits He conferred upon them, He says that He was not known to them by His name “Jehovah;” signifying thus that He now more brightly manifested the glory of His divinity to their descendants. It would be tedious to recount the various opinions as to the name “Jehovah.” It is certainly a foul superstition of the Jews that they dare not speak, or write it, but substitute the name “Adonai;” nor do I any more approve of their teaching, who say that it is <hi type="italic">ineffable</hi>, because it is not written according to grammatical rule. Without controversy, it is derived from the word <foreign xml:lang="he">היה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">hayah</hi>, or <foreign xml:lang="he">הוה</foreign>, <hi type="italic">havah</hi>, and therefore it is rightly said by learned commentators to be the essential name of God, whereas others are, as it were, epithets. Since, then, nothing is more peculiar to God than eternity, He is called Jehovah, because He has existence from Himself, and sustains all things by His secret inspiration. Nor do I agree with the grammarians, who will not have it pronounced, because its inflection is irregular; because its etymology, of which all confess that God is the author, is more to me than an hundred rules. <note n="72"> <div sID="gen6895" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">A</hi>.<hi type="italic"> Pfeiffer</hi> in his <hi type="italic">Dubia vexata</hi>, rightly observes upon this passage. The name Jehovah was not, strictly and literally, unknown to the fathers, but it was so, in respect of the perfect fulfillment of the promises implied in it; more especially, that glorious one of the deliverance out of Egypt.” —<hi type="italic"> Rosenmuller in Brightwell</hi>. “Prior to that time, the name <hi type="italic">Jehovah </hi>had been often used to describe the existence, the necessity, or the unchangeableness of God; but now, to indicate His faithfulness, His truth and constancy, in keeping and fulfilling His promises.” —<hi type="italic"> Dathe in loco</hi>.<hi type="italic"> Holden</hi>, however, and others, would elude the difficulty by reading the clause interrogatively. He says, “It is impossible to read the history of Abraham, etc., without being convinced that both the name of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, and the attributes implied by that name, were known to them. Our <hi type="italic">A</hi>.<hi type="italic">V</hi>., therefore, must be erroneous. Now every difficulty will be removed by reading it interrogatively, ‘And by my name Jehovah was I not known to them?’ which is both agreeable to the Hebrew idiom, and to the scope of the context.”<div eID="gen6895" type="x-p"/> </note> Nor does God by “His name” in this passage mean syllables or letters, but the knowledge of His glory and majesty, which shone out more fully and more brightly in the redemption of His Church, than in the commencement of the covenant. For Abraham and the other Patriarchs were content with a smaller measure of light; whence it follows that the fault of their descendants would be less excusable, if their faith was not answerable to the increase of their grace. Meanwhile, Moses is awakened to activity whilst God is setting before him a magnificent and singular means of shewing forth His glory.<div eID="gen6894" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen6893" osisID="Exod.6.2" type="section"/>
entries.4752080f3c880edc6b1ab9e3ba59fce1fe82ea62: <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Exod.6.4" sID="gen6896" type="section"/> <div sID="gen6897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I have also established my covenant.</hi> The hope of the deliverance which He had formerly promised, and which the Patriarchs had expected, He confirms by alluding to the covenant, as I have just above said; and the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">גם</foreign>, <hi type="italic">gam</hi>, which is twice repeated, is, in the first case, <hi type="italic">causal</hi>, in the second, <hi type="italic">illative</hi>, as much as to say, “Since I covenanted with your fathers, therefore I have now determined to bring you into the land of Canaan;” unless it be preferred to resolve it thus, “I, the same who established the covenant with your fathers, now also have heard your groaning.” Moreover, because the covenant is founded on free grace, God commands the redemption to be expected as much from His good pleasure as from His steadfastness. But He again commends the faith of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because they patiently consented to be strangers and pilgrims in the land of Canaan, which by the covenant of God was their own lawful inheritance. For it was a proof of their exemplary virtue, to be wanderers all their lives, and not to have a single corner to put their foot upon, unless what was granted them by sufferance for the erection of their tents, being at the mercy of their neighbors; as natives are always apt to despise strangers. And by this comparison the slowness of heart and ingratitude of their posterity is the more condemned, if they refuse to take possession of this land, which was so earnestly desired by their holy fathers, and at the sight of which alone they counted themselves blessed, although they were only sojourners there.<div eID="gen6897" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Exod.6.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen6896" osisID="Exod.6.4" type="section"/>
